subject: ZEMAN et al. (1959)
object: ZEMAN et al. (1959) studied the hereditary pattern of idiopathic dystonia musculorum deformans.

subject: ZEMAN et al. (1960)
object: ZEMAN et al. (1960) reported on the formes frustes (incomplete or mild forms) of idiopathic dystonia musculorum deformans.

subject: Zeman and Dyken (1967)
object: Zeman and Dyken (1967) reported clinical, genetic and pathoanatomical studies of dystonia musculorum deformans.

subject: Yanagisawa et al. (1972)
object: Yanagisawa et al. (1972) reported familial dystonia musculorum deformans occurring together with tremor.

subject: Wooten et al. (1973)
object: Wooten et al. (1973) reported elevated plasma dopamine-beta-hydroxylase activity in autosomal dominant torsion dystonia.

subject: Bundey et al. (1975)
object: Bundey et al. (1975) carried out a family study of 32 patients with torsion dystonia. They identified at least 2 forms of generalized dystonia with onset in childhood, one autosomal dominant and one autosomal recessive, and the 2 forms could not be told apart clinically. At least 3 families and probably about 6 to 8 patients had the autosomal recessive form.

subject: Bundey et al. (1975)
object: Bundey et al. (1975) suggested that the remaining 9 to 11 patients with generalized childhood-onset dystonia were new dominant mutations, because there appeared to be a paternal age effect. Since fitness in patients with childhood onset was 1/20 of normal, most childhood dominant cases appeared sporadically.

subject: Bundey et al. (1975)
object: Bundey et al. (1975) found that most of the other 15 patients, 12 of whom had onset in adult life, appeared to have a non-genetic torsion dystonia. However, they observed one example of a benign adult-onset dominant form associated with tremor. They concluded that there are at least 2 genetic forms of torsion dystonia: an autosomal recessive childhood-onset form and one or more dominant forms with onset in childhood or adult life.

subject: Ziegler et al. (1976)
object: Ziegler et al. (1976) measured plasma norepinephrine and dopamine-beta-hydroxylase in patients with dystonia.

subject: Askenasy et al. (1980)
object: Askenasy et al. (1980) studied 13 Ashkenazi Jewish patients with torsion dystonia of various origins, together with their families. Patients and their relatives had significantly higher serum dopamine-beta-hydroxylase (DBH) activity than controls, particularly in the childhood-onset group. Jewish origin, dominant inheritance, slow progression and axial distribution were each not specific for an elevated serum DBH activity.

subject: Askenasy et al. (1980)
object: Askenasy et al. (1980) found that an intravenous injection of 20 mg metoclopramide did not change serum DBH activity in 12 patients with torsion dystonia or in 17 relatives. In 1 patient with symptomatic dystonia and 2 of her maternal relatives (who had different fathers), serum DBH activity doubled or tripled after the injection. The authors suggested that a metoclopramide-induced rise in serum DBH activity in relatives of torsion dystonia patients indicates a genetic predisposition.

subject: Eldridge (1981)
object: Eldridge (1981) addressed the mode of inheritance of torsion dystonia in Jews.

subject: Lorden et al. (1984)
object: Lorden et al. (1984) described an autosomal recessive neurologic disorder, named dystonic (dt), in Sprague-Dawley rats, characterized by sustained twisting movements during waking. Mutants were indistinguishable from normal littermates before postnatal days 9 to 10; signs beginning on day 10 included twisting of the axial musculature, hyperflexion of the trunk, self-clasping of forelimbs and hindlimbs, and poor limb placement during locomotion. No morphologic lesions of neural or non-neural tissues were seen with routine light microscopy.

subject: Lorden et al. (1984)
object: Lorden et al. (1984) found that dt rats had significantly elevated cerebellar norepinephrine levels, with normal levels in other locus ceruleus terminal fields and no difference in cerebellar noradrenergic innervation by histochemical fluorescence. The mutants were less sensitive to the akinesic effects of haloperidol, although striatal dopamine levels were not reliably different and apomorphine responses appeared normal. The authors suggested biochemical disturbances in the extrapyramidal system and proposed the dt rat as a model for human dystonia musculorum deformans.

subject: Zilber et al. (1984)
object: Zilber et al. (1984) analyzed data from a nationwide survey of idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD) in Israel. They identified 47 patients between 1969 and 1980, 40 of them of European origin. Among European Jews, ITD frequency was about 1 in 23,000 live births, about 5 times higher than in Jews of Afro-Asian origin.

subject: Zilber et al. (1984)
object: Zilber et al. (1984) assumed that all ITD cases in their Israeli Jewish series fit one genetic model. Under that assumption, X-linked and simple autosomal recessive models did not fit the data well. An autosomal dominant model with low penetrance could account for the observations and gave an estimated ITD gene frequency of 3 to 4 per 100,000 in European Jews. Multifactorial inheritance was also possible. The authors cautioned that it may be inappropriate to assume all cases share the same genetic basis, or even that all are inherited.

subject: Zilber et al. (1984)
object: Zilber et al. (1984) found that fathers of isolated ITD cases were older than expected. Based on this, they suggested that some isolated cases may have been new mutations.

subject: Batshaw et al. (1985)
object: Batshaw et al. (1985) reported that Munchausen's syndrome can simulate torsion dystonia, which makes it a consideration in the differential diagnosis.

subject: Hornykiewicz et al. (1986)
object: Hornykiewicz et al. (1986) examined the brains of 2 patients with generalized childhood-onset dystonia musculorum deformans after death. Histology showed no important changes in the basal ganglia, cerebral cortex, higher brainstem nuclei, locus ceruleus, or raphe nuclei. Choline acetyltransferase activity and the levels of GABA and glutamic acid in the cortex and basal ganglia were within the control range. Norepinephrine concentrations were markedly and consistently decreased in the lateral and posterior hypothalamus, mamillary body, subthalamic nucleus, and locus ceruleus. Serotonin was subnormal in the dorsal raphe nucleus, dopamine was low in the nucleus accumbens (and in the striatum in 1 of the 2 cases), and norepinephrine, serotonin, and 5-HIAA were raised in several other regions.

subject: Hornykiewicz et al. (1986)
object: Hornykiewicz et al. (1986) concluded that some of the monoamine changes they found may represent a basic neurochemical abnormality in dystonia musculorum deformans, especially the pronounced apparent disturbance of noradrenergic brain mechanisms. They suggested these changes may be relevant to the disorder's pathophysiology and treatment.

subject: Breakefield et al. (1986)
object: Breakefield et al. (1986) performed linkage analysis with restriction fragment length polymorphisms in a family with autosomal dominant torsion dystonia in which more than 50 members had neurologic examination. Using LOD score analysis that allowed for age of onset and incomplete penetrance, they excluded the pro-opiomelanocortin and glutamic acid decarboxylase genes, which had been implicated in rat models, as well as other genomic regions, as the site of the disease gene in this family.

subject: Breakefield et al. (1986)
object: Breakefield et al. (1986) studied a family in which torsion dystonia showed autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance.

subject: Kramer et al. (1987)
object: Kramer et al. (1987) performed multipoint linkage analysis of autosomal dominant torsion dystonia in a single large non-Jewish pedigree using linkage groups on chromosomes 11p, 13q, and 21q. They excluded large portions of chromosomes 11p and 13q and virtually the entire long arm of chromosome 21 from linkage with dystonia.

subject: Ozelius et al. (1989)
object: Ozelius et al. (1989) used linkage analysis with polymorphic DNA and protein markers in a large non-Jewish kindred with torsion dystonia. They found that the dystonia gene (ITD1) was tightly linked to the gelsolin gene. Multipoint linkage analysis placed it in the 9q32-q34 region, between ABO and D9S26, a region that also contains the dopamine-beta-hydroxylase locus.

subject: Ozelius et al. (1989)
object: Ozelius et al. (1989) reported that affected members of a large non-Jewish kindred with torsion dystonia had a clinical syndrome similar to the one seen in the Ashkenazi Jewish population. Torsion dystonia is characterized by loss of control of voluntary movements, appearing as sustained muscle contractions and/or abnormal postures.

subject: Ozelius et al. (1989)
object: Ozelius et al. (1989) noted that most of the hereditary forms of torsion dystonia described so far show autosomal dominant transmission with variable expressivity.

subject: Ozelius et al. (1989)
object: Ozelius et al. (1989) stated that the frequency of the defective torsion dystonia gene in the Ashkenazi Jewish population is about 1 in 10,000.

subject: Bressman et al. (1989)
object: Bressman et al. (1989) studied the families of 43 Ashkenazi Jewish probands whose idiopathic torsion dystonia began before age 28 years. They examined 146 first-degree and 96 second-degree relatives; 19 relatives had definite dystonia and 2 had probable dystonia. Counting definite cases only, the age-adjusted risk was 15.5% for first-degree relatives and 6.5% for second-degree relatives. Risk did not differ significantly by sex, or between parents, offspring and sibs. Using maximum likelihood analysis, the authors found the risks consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance, with penetrance estimated at 29.4% for definite cases or 32.2% when probable cases were included.

subject: Bressman et al. (1989)
object: Assuming a disease frequency of 1 in 15,000 among Ashkenazi Jews, Bressman et al. (1989) estimated the gene frequency for idiopathic torsion dystonia at 1 in 9,000.

subject: Risch et al. (1990)
object: Risch et al. (1990) carried out segregation analysis in a family study of idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi Jews. The study included 43 probands with onset before age 27 years from 42 nuclear families. The pedigrees were extended through all available first- and second-degree relatives, who were examined directly and videotaped. Final diagnoses were based on the examination findings and a blinded review of the videotapes. The data were consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with 30% penetrance. Recessive and polygenic inheritance were strongly rejected, and there was no evidence for sporadic cases or new mutations.

subject: Risch et al. (1990)
object: Risch et al. (1990) suggested that the high incidence and dominant inheritance of early-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi Jews pointed to genetic homogeneity within this population. They proposed that this would make the population especially useful for linkage studies.

subject: Kramer et al. (1990)
object: Kramer et al. (1990) used linkage analysis with DNA polymorphisms in 12 Ashkenazi Jewish families with idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD). They found that the dystonia gene was closely linked to the argininosuccinate synthetase gene (ASS). Multipoint analysis placed it in the 9q32-q34 region, which also contains the gelsolin and dopamine-beta-hydroxylase loci.

subject: Kramer et al. (1990)
object: Kramer et al. (1990) suggested that the same gene may cause ITD both in a previously reported non-Jewish kindred linked to 9q32-34 and in the Ashkenazi Jewish families they studied. Because penetrance of the dominant allele differed substantially between the 2 groups, they suggested that 2 different mutations may produce susceptibility to the disease in the 2 groups.

subject: Kramer et al. (1990)
object: Kramer et al. (1990) noted that ITD is 5 to 10 times more frequent in the Ashkenazi Jewish population than in other groups.

subject: Kramer et al. (1990)
object: Kramer et al. (1990) described idiopathic torsion dystonia as a neurologic disorder of sustained muscle contractions. These appear as twisting movements of the limbs, trunk, and/or neck and can progress to abnormal postures. Most familial forms follow autosomal dominant transmission with reduced penetrance.

subject: Müller and Kupke (1990)
object: In a review, Müller and Kupke (1990) stated that primary torsion dystonia may be inherited as an autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked recessive trait, and that at least six forms of autosomal dominant torsion dystonia can be distinguished clinically.

subject: Müller and Kupke (1990)
object: Müller and Kupke (1990) reviewed linkage analysis in one form of autosomal dominant torsion dystonia that assigned a 'torsion dystonia locus' to the long arm of chromosome 9.

subject: Müller and Kupke (1990)
object: Müller and Kupke (1990) described primary torsion dystonia as an idiopathic movement disorder presumably caused by abnormal function of the basal ganglia.

subject: Kwiatkowski et al. (1991)
object: Using GT repeat polymorphisms from the 9q32-34 region, Kwiatkowski et al. (1991) localized the gene causing idiopathic torsion dystonia in Ashkenazi Jewish families to the 11-cM interval between AK1 and D9S10. The authors stated that no candidate genes were known in this region.

subject: Kwiatkowski et al. (1991)
object: Kwiatkowski et al. (1991) found that linkage analysis in a large non-Jewish family was also consistent with the dystonia gene lying in the 9q32-34 region, although positive lod scores in that family extended over an interval of more than 20 cM.

subject: Kwiatkowski et al. (1991)
object: Kwiatkowski et al. (1991) described idiopathic torsion dystonia as sustained, involuntary muscle contractions that often cause twisting and repetitive movements or abnormal postures. They noted that most familial forms show autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance.

subject: Ozelius et al. (1992)
object: Ozelius et al. (1992) used (GT)n and RFLP markers on chromosome 9q32-34 and identified obligate recombination events in Ashkenazi Jewish families with early-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia, narrowing the DYT1 region to a 6-cM interval bounded by AK1 and ASS. Based on obligate recombinants, DYT1 was placed centromeric to ASS, and allelic association predicted that DYT1, ABL, and ASS lie within 1-2 cM of each other.

subject: Ozelius et al. (1992)
object: Ozelius et al. (1992) found highly significant linkage disequilibrium between DYT1 and an extended ABL-ASS haplotype in 52 unrelated affected Ashkenazi Jewish individuals: the 4/A12 haplotype was present on 69% of disease-bearing chromosomes versus 1% of control Jewish chromosomes (chi-square = 91.07). The authors concluded that a single mutation event is responsible for most hereditary cases of dystonia in the Jewish population.

subject: Ozelius et al. (1992)
object: Ozelius et al. (1992) found that of 53 definitely affected Ashkenazi Jewish individuals typed, 13 appeared sporadic, yet a similar proportion of sporadic (8/13, 62%) and familial (28/40, 70%) cases carried the ASS A12 haplotype. They suggested that many sporadic cases are hereditary, that the disease gene frequency is greater than 1/15,000, and that penetrance is lower than the previously estimated 30%; most affected individuals were heterozygous for the ABL-ASS haplotype, supporting autosomal dominant inheritance.

subject: Ozelius et al. (1992)
object: Ozelius et al. (1992) proposed that ABL-ASS extended-haplotype status would provide predictive value for DYT1 carrier status in Jewish individuals and could be used for molecular diagnosis.

subject: Warner et al. (1993)
object: Warner et al. (1993) performed linkage analysis in 27 small families with idiopathic torsion dystonia (26 British and 1 French; 3 Ashkenazi Jewish), using the highly polymorphic 9q34 loci ASS and ABL. The cumulative lod score for ASS at a recombination fraction of 0.001 was -6.72. HOMOG analysis nevertheless gave evidence for linkage of an idiopathic torsion dystonia gene to 9q34 in a subset of families. The authors concluded that a locus at 9q34 exists in both Jewish and non-Jewish kindreds in the UK.

subject: Warner et al. (1993)
object: Warner et al. (1993) found that lod scores in 3 non-Jewish families excluded a disease locus tightly linked to ASS on 9q34, although these families were clinically indistinguishable from the others. HOMOG analysis showed significant heterogeneity. The authors suggested that idiopathic torsion dystonia is genetically heterogeneous.

subject: Warner et al. (1993)
object: Warner et al. (1993) found the same allelic association between ASS/ABL and idiopathic torsion dystonia in British Jewish kindreds that had been reported in Ashkenazi Jewish families in the USA.

subject: Bressman et al. (1994)
object: Bressman et al. (1994) studied 174 Ashkenazi Jewish individuals with idiopathic torsion dystonia, classifying them by a DYT1-associated haplotype of 9q34 markers (D9S62, D9S63, ASS) into 90 carriers, 70 noncarriers, and 14 ambiguous individuals. Mean age at onset was significantly lower in carriers than noncarriers (12.5 +/- 8.2 vs 36.5 +/- 16.4 years). In 94% of carriers symptoms began in a limb (arm or leg equally), and onset in the neck (3.3%) or larynx (2.2%) was rare.

subject: Bressman et al. (1994)
object: Bressman et al. (1994) found that among Ashkenazi Jewish dystonia patients not carrying the DYT1-associated haplotype, the neck, larynx, and other cranial muscles were the sites of onset in 79%, arm onset occurred in 21%, and leg onset never occurred. Limb onset, leg involvement during the disease course, and age at onset distinguished haplotype carriers from noncarriers with 90% accuracy.

subject: Bressman et al. (1994)
object: Bressman et al. (1994) noted that linkage disequilibrium between DYT1 and a particular 9q34 haplotype in Ashkenazi Jews implies that a large proportion of early-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia in this population is due to a founder mutation in DYT1.

subject: Kramer et al. (1994)
object: Kramer et al. (1994) studied 7 non-Jewish families with idiopathic torsion dystonia of northern European and French Canadian descent. Their results were consistent with linkage to the DYT1 region on chromosome 9q34.

subject: Kramer et al. (1994)
object: Kramer et al. (1994) found that affected members of 7 non-Jewish families linked to DYT1 were clinically similar to Ashkenazi Jewish cases. Onset was mainly in the limbs, and in each pedigree at least 1 person had onset before age 12 years.

subject: Kramer et al. (1994)
object: Kramer et al. (1994) reported that none of the affected individuals in the non-Jewish families carried the Ashkenazi Jewish DYT1 haplotype. They concluded that these families probably have different mutations in the DYT1 gene. The 2 French Canadian families shared the same haplotype.

subject: Kramer et al. (1994)
object: Kramer et al. (1994) estimated penetrance in the non-Jewish families at 0.40 to 0.75. After identifying disease gene carriers and adjusting for age at onset, they obtained a direct penetrance estimate of 0.46. This was consistent with the 30 to 40% estimated in the Ashkenazi Jewish population.

subject: Kramer et al. (1994)
object: Kramer et al. (1994) found that 2 other non-Jewish families with atypical idiopathic torsion dystonia, meaning later onset and/or cranial or cervical involvement, were not linked to DYT1. They took this as evidence that other genes are involved in dystonia.

subject: Kramer et al. (1994)
object: Kramer et al. (1994) noted that in the Ashkenazi Jewish population there is strong linkage disequilibrium between DYT1 and nearby markers within a 2-cM region. The associated haplotype is present in more than 90% of early limb-onset Ashkenazi Jewish cases.

subject: Zoossmann-Diskin (1995)
object: Zoossmann-Diskin (1995) discussed whether genetic drift or selection accounts for idiopathic torsion dystonia (ITD) in the Ashkenazi Jewish population.

subject: Risch et al. (1995)
object: Risch et al. (1995) analyzed six closely linked microsatellite loci on chromosome 9q34 in 59 Ashkenazi Jewish families with idiopathic torsion dystonia. They concluded that a single founder mutation accounts for most (more than 90%) of early-onset cases in the Ashkenazi population. They estimated that this mutation first appeared about 350 years ago.

subject: Risch et al. (1995)
object: Risch et al. (1995) found that carriers of the founder mutation tended to come from the northern part of the historic Jewish Pale of Settlement (Lithuania and Byelorussia). They estimated the current frequency of this dominant mutation at between 1/6,000 and 1/2,000. They suggested that the mutation's recent origin and high frequency mean the Ashkenazi population descends from a limited group of founders, and they emphasized the role of genetic drift.

subject: Gasser et al. (1996)
object: Gasser et al. (1996) determined haplotypes at 5 marker loci closely linked to DYT1 on chromosome 9q in 10 Ashkenazi Jewish patients with focal hand dystonia (8 with musician's cramp and 2 with writer's cramp). The founder haplotype associated with more than 90% of generalized dystonia cases in the Ashkenazi Jewish population could not be constructed from any of the 20 chromosomes, and no common haplotype was seen. The authors concluded that these findings argued against a role for the DYT1 founder mutation in occupational hand dystonia in this population. They also concluded that if DYT1 is involved in these later-onset dystonias, there was no evidence for a common mutation.

subject: Gasser et al. (1996)
object: Gasser et al. (1996) suggested that excessive repetitive use, possibly combined with ulnar neuropathy, may trigger some focal dystonias.

subject: Cheng et al. (1996)
object: Cheng et al. (1996) studied 260 probands with idiopathic adult-onset cranial or cervical dystonia. Their mean age at onset was 45.71 +/- 15.85 years. Forty-nine probands had a positive family history of dystonia or tremor in first- or second-degree relatives, and 7 had affected siblings only. Postural or action tremor was frequent in patients and relatives, which the authors took as evidence that tremor is part of the clinical manifestation of dystonia.

subject: Cheng et al. (1996)
object: In a retrospective analysis of 49 families with adult-onset cranial or cervical dystonia, Cheng et al. (1996) found that age at onset was on average 21.25 years earlier in the second generation than in the first (p = 1.11 x 10(-8)). The authors suggested that this was compatible with genetic anticipation and that an unstable trinucleotide repeat is most likely involved in adult-onset primary cranial or cervical dystonia.

subject: Ozelius et al. (1997)
object: Ozelius et al. (1997) built a YAC contig covering 600 kb of the 2-cM region between D9S62a and ASS on chromosome 9q34. They added new polymorphic loci to the linkage disequilibrium analysis of the Ashkenazi Jewish founder mutation and placed the DYT1 gene most likely within a 150-kb region between D9S2161 and D9S63.

subject: Ozelius et al. (1997)
object: Ozelius et al. (1997) stated that early-onset torsion dystonia due to DYT1 is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with reduced penetrance of 30 to 40%. They noted that DYT1 appears to account for most cases of early-onset torsion dystonia in both Ashkenazi Jewish and non-Jewish families.

subject: Ozelius et al. (1997)
object: Ozelius et al. (1997) noted that the abnormal involuntary movements of torsion dystonia are believed to be caused by unbalanced neural transmission in the basal ganglia.

subject: Ozelius et al. (1997)
object: Ozelius et al. (1997) identified the DYT1 gene on chromosome 9q34 as the gene responsible for autosomal dominant early-onset torsion dystonia. They found that almost all cases of early-onset dystonia carried a unique 3-bp deletion, which results in loss of one of a pair of glutamic acid residues in a conserved region of torsinA, a novel ATP-binding protein. The deletion appeared to have arisen independently in different ethnic populations.

subject: TOR1A 3-bp deletion resulting in loss of one of a pair of glutamic-acid residues
object: TOR1A

subject: Ozelius et al. (1997)
object: Ozelius et al. (1997) concluded that the recurrent 3-bp DYT1 deletion appeared to have arisen independently in different ethnic populations.

subject: Ozelius et al. (1997)
object: Ozelius et al. (1997) described early-onset torsion dystonia as a movement disorder that begins in childhood and is characterized by twisting muscle contractures. Symptoms were believed to result from altered neuronal communication in the basal ganglia.

subject: Ozelius et al. (1997)
object: Ozelius et al. (1997) found that torsinA, the DYT1 gene product, is a novel ATP-binding protein. It has homologs in nematode, rat, mouse and humans and shows some resemblance to the heat-shock protein and Clp protease families.

subject: Müller et al. (1998)
object: In a review of the clinical and molecular genetics of primary dystonias, Müller et al. (1998) proposed naming the known forms dystonias 1-12. They noted that most of these forms can be told apart by genetic criteria, with autosomal dominant idiopathic torsion dystonia designated DYT1.

subject: Müller et al. (1998)
object: Müller et al. (1998) reviewed the gene loci found in autosomal dominant primary dystonias, including idiopathic torsion dystonia on 9q34. They also reported that mutations in a gene coding for an ATP-binding protein had been detected in idiopathic torsion dystonia (DYT1).

subject: Kamm et al. (1999)
object: Kamm et al. (1999) screened 57 German patients with idiopathic torsion dystonia for the 3-bp GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene. They found it in 3 of 5 patients with early limb-onset dystonia, one of whom had a positive family history, and in 1 young patient with multifocal dystonia and a short disease course.

subject: TOR1A 3-bp GAG deletion
object: TOR1A

subject: Kamm et al. (1999)
object: Kamm et al. (1999) did not find the GAG deletion in 2 patients with early-onset generalized dystonia that began in the cervical muscles, or in 5 other patients with multifocal, 14 with segmental, and 30 with focal cervical dystonia. They suggested that in their population the deletion accounts for a major portion of typical early limb-onset dystonia but not for other types of dystonia.

subject: Ikeuchi et al. (1999)
object: Ikeuchi et al. (1999) reported a Japanese patient with primary torsion dystonia who carried the 3-bp (GAG) deletion in the DYT1 gene. The authors described the patient's clinical presentation as unique.

subject: TOR1A 3-bp (GAG) deletion
object: TOR1A

subject: Valente et al. (1999)
object: Valente et al. (1999) analyzed haplotypes around the DYT1 gene in 9 Ashkenazi Jewish (AJ) British patients with the GAG deletion. All of them carried the same haplotype as North American AJ patients. The authors took this as support for the theory that the current British AJ community descends from the same small group of individuals as North American Jewry.

subject: Valente et al. (1999)
object: Among 15 non-Jewish British patients with the DYT1 GAG deletion, Valente et al. (1999) found only a limited number of distinct founder haplotypes. They concluded that the GAG deletion is not a very frequent mutation and has arisen only a limited number of times over the centuries.

subject: Leung et al. (2001)
object: Leung et al. (2001) found an 18-bp deletion in the TOR1A gene (Phe323_Tyr328del) in a patient with early onset dystonia and myoclonic features. The deletion was predicted to remove 6 amino acids close to the carboxy terminus of torsinA, including a putative phosphorylation site. The authors stated that this was the first TOR1A mutation identified besides the GAG deletion (Glu302/303del), and that it was associated with a distinct type of early onset dystonia.

subject: TOR1A p.F323
object: TOR1A

subject: Leung et al. (2001)
object: Leung et al. (2001) screened TOR1A in 40 patients with early onset dystonia or early onset parkinsonism (EOP) and found 3 variations, none in EOP patients. Two infrequent intronic single-bp changes of unknown consequence were found in a dystonia patient and in the mother of an EOP patient.

subject: Németh (2002)
object: In a review, Németh (2002) described the dystonias as a heterogeneous group of disorders with a strong inherited basis. The review covered primary dystonias, including idiopathic torsion dystonia (DYT1), as well as 'dystonia-plus' syndromes and heredodegenerative disorders, with a focus on their clinical and genetic features and molecular mechanisms.

subject: Hjermind et al. (2002)
object: Hjermind et al. (2002) screened 107 Danish probands with primary torsion dystonia for the GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene, after secondary dystonia had been excluded clinically and biochemically. They found the mutation in 3 probands, all of whom had the classical DYT1 phenotype. None of the probands with other types of dystonia carried the GAG deletion.

subject: TOR1A GAG-deletion
object: TOR1A

subject: Hjermind et al. (2002)
object: Hjermind et al. (2002) described 2 of the 3 Danish DYT1 GAG-deletion carriers who were apparently sporadic cases. In one, the mutation had arisen de novo. In the other, a parent was an asymptomatic carrier. The authors noted that de novo mutations in the DYT1 gene are seldom reported, although independent founder mutations are known to have occurred.

subject: Hjermind et al. (2002)
object: Hjermind et al. (2002) found DYT1 dystonia to be uncommon among Danish probands with primary torsion dystonia (3 of 107), even though several probands had early-onset generalized dystonia.

subject: Bressman et al. (2002)
object: Bressman et al. (2002) evaluated the hierarchical diagnostic categories of definite, probable, and possible dystonia used in family studies by assessing 147 DYT1 GAG deletion carriers and 113 blood-related noncarriers from 43 families. Only the category of definite dystonia was 100% specific; probable dystonia, but not possible dystonia, was increased in carriers compared with noncarriers. The authors recommended that only individuals with definite signs of dystonia be considered affected in linkage and other genetic studies.

subject: TOR1A DYT1 GAG deletion
object: TOR1A

subject: Ghilardi et al. (2003)
object: Ghilardi et al. (2003) compared movement and sequence learning in 12 clinically unaffected DYT1 mutation carriers with 12 age-matched controls. Motor performance did not differ between groups (no significant differences in movement time or spatial accuracy), but sequence learning was reduced in gene carriers relative to controls (p < 0.01). The authors suggested that abnormalities in motor behavior exist in clinically nonmanifesting DYT1 carriers.

subject: Ghilardi et al. (2003)
object: Ghilardi et al. (2003) used H2(15)O PET during task performance in nonmanifesting DYT1 carriers. During motor execution, carriers showed increased activation in the left premotor cortex and right supplementary motor area, with reduced activation in the posterior medial cerebellum; during sequence learning, activation was increased in the left ventral prefrontal cortex and lateral cerebellum. The authors suggested that localized increases in neural activity may enable normal movement execution in carriers but may not compensate for their defect in sequence learning.

subject: Grundmann et al. (2003)
object: Grundmann et al. (2003) screened 256 patients with different subtypes of dystonia from 4 movement disorder outpatient clinics in Germany for the GAG deletion in the DYT1 gene using PCR. They found the deletion in 6 of the 256 patients.

subject: TOR1A 3-base pair (GAG) deletion
object: TOR1A

subject: Grundmann et al. (2003)
object: Grundmann et al. (2003) found that only 2 of the 6 GAG deletion carriers had classic early-onset primary generalized dystonia. Two carriers had multifocal dystonia, 1 of them with involvement of cranial and cervical muscles, and 2 had writer's cramp of both hands with only slight progression. The authors concluded that the mutation may be associated with segmental and multifocal as well as generalized dystonia, and that this phenotypic variability may make it difficult to predict carrier status and to give genetic counseling.

subject: TOR1A GAG deletion
object: TOR1A

subject: Carbon et al. (2004)
object: Carbon et al. (2004) used FDG PET to scan 12 nonmanifesting and 11 manifesting DYT1 gene carriers, 6 nonmanifesting and 7 manifesting DYT6 gene carriers, and 11 controls. Manifesting carriers of both genotypes showed bilateral hypermetabolism in the presupplementary motor area (Brodmann area 6) and parietal association cortices (BA 40/7) compared with nonmanifesting counterparts, whereas DYT1 carriers showed genotype-specific increases in metabolism in the putamen, anterior cingulate (BA 24/32), and cerebellar hemispheres. The authors suggested that clinical manifestations are related to cortical dysfunction, while subcortical metabolic abnormalities may represent genotype-specific trait features, and that dystonia may be associated with abnormal movement preparation caused by defective sensorimotor integration.

subject: Carbon et al. (2004)
object: Carbon et al. (2004) found that, in contrast to DYT1 carriers, genotype-specific changes in DYT6 carriers involved hypometabolism of the putamen and hypermetabolism in the temporal cortex (BA 21), indicating distinct subcortical metabolic signatures for the 2 dystonia genotypes.

subject: Carbon et al. (2004)
object: Carbon et al. (2004) used diffusion tensor MRI to study white matter pathways in DYT1 mutation carriers and control subjects. Fractional anisotropy, a measure of axonal integrity and coherence, was reduced (p < 0.005) in the subgyral white matter of the sensorimotor cortex of DYT1 carriers. The authors suggested that abnormal anatomical connectivity of the supplementary motor area may contribute to the susceptibility of DYT1 carriers to develop clinical manifestations of dystonia.

subject: Heiman et al. (2004)
object: Heiman et al. (2004) gave a standardized psychiatric interview to members of families with an identified DYT1 mutation. They compared 96 mutation carriers with dystonia, 60 carriers without dystonia, and 65 noncarriers. Compared with noncarriers, the risk of recurrent major depressive disorder was higher in nonmanifesting carriers (RR = 4.95, CI 1.72-14.29) and in manifesting carriers (RR = 3.62, CI 1.00-10.53). Carriers also developed recurrent depression at an earlier age.

subject: Heiman et al. (2004)
object: Heiman et al. (2004) found that how severe the motor signs were did not predict the likelihood of recurrent depression in DYT1 mutation carriers. Carriers did not have a higher risk of other affective disorders, such as single major depression or bipolar disorder. The authors concluded that early-onset recurrent major depression is associated with the DYT1 GAG mutation independently of motor symptoms, and suggested that it is a clinical expression of the mutation.

subject: McNaught et al. (2004)
object: McNaught et al. (2004) described perinuclear inclusion bodies in the midbrain reticular formation and periaqueductal gray in 4 clinically documented and genetically confirmed DYT1 patients but not in controls. The inclusions were located within cholinergic and other neurons in the pedunculopontine nucleus, cuneiform nucleus, and griseum centrale mesencephali, and stained positively for ubiquitin, torsinA, and the nuclear envelope protein lamin A/C. No inclusion bodies were detected in the substantia nigra pars compacta, striatum, hippocampus, or selected regions of the cerebral cortex.

subject: McNaught et al. (2004)
object: McNaught et al. (2004) also noted tau/ubiquitin-immunoreactive aggregates in pigmented neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta and locus ceruleus in all 4 DYT1 dystonia cases but not in controls. The authors concluded that the findings supported the notion that DYT1 dystonia is associated with impaired protein handling and the nuclear envelope, and suggested that alterations in the pedunculopontine and cuneiform nuclei and related brainstem structures, which mediate motor activity and muscle tone, could underlie the pathophysiology of DYT1 dystonia.

subject: Shashidharan et al. (2005)
object: Shashidharan et al. (2005) generated 4 independent lines of transgenic mice overexpressing human DeltaE-torsinA under a neuron-specific enolase promoter. As early as 3 weeks after birth, the mice developed abnormal involuntary movements with dystonic-appearing self-clasping of the limbs, as well as hyperkinesia and rapid bidirectional circling. About 40% of the transgenic mice in each line showed these severe behavioral abnormalities.

subject: Shashidharan et al. (2005)
object: In the DeltaE-torsinA transgenic mice, Shashidharan et al. (2005) found decreased striatal dopamine in behaviorally affected animals but increased levels in transgenic mice without behavioral changes. Immunohistochemistry showed perinuclear inclusions and aggregates that stained for ubiquitin, torsinA, and lamin, a nuclear envelope marker. These inclusions were in neurons of the pedunculopontine nucleus and other brainstem regions, in a pattern similar to that described in DYT1 patients.

subject: Asanuma et al. (2005)
object: Asanuma et al. (2005) used PET with [11C]-raclopride to study non-manifesting carriers of the DYT1 mutation. Striatal D2 receptor binding was reduced by about 15% in the caudate and putamen (p < 0.005). The authors suggested that reduced striatal D2 binding is a trait feature of the DYT1 genotype.

subject: Kostić et al. (2006)
object: Kostić et al. (2006) described a large Serbian family in which the DYT1 phenotype varied widely within the family, from asymptomatic carrier status to late-onset focal dystonia and generalized jerky dystonia.

subject: Kostić et al. (2006)
object: In a large Serbian family, Kostić et al. (2006) identified 7 carriers of the 3-bp (GAG) deletion in the DYT1 gene. Six carriers were confirmed by direct analysis and 1 was inferred from haplotype. Only 2 of the carriers had dystonia, giving a penetrance of 29%.

subject: Kostić et al. (2006)
object: Kostić et al. (2006) found that 3 members of the same Serbian family who did not carry the GAG deletion also developed dystonia: 2 had multifocal dystonia and 1 had torticollis. The authors suggested that these involuntary movements were caused by some other factor, such as another dystonia gene, or might be psychogenic.

subject: Risch et al. (2007)
object: Risch et al. (2007) genotyped 3 DYT1 SNPs, including the coding variant D216H, in DYT1 GAG-deletion carriers with dystonia (n=119), GAG-deletion carriers without dystonia (n=113), and controls (n=197). Compared with controls, the 216H allele was more frequent in nonmanifesting carriers and less frequent in carriers with dystonia. In haplotype analysis, the H allele in trans with the GAG deletion was highly protective, and there was suggestive evidence that the D216 allele in cis is required for the disease to be penetrant. The authors concluded that this was the first clinically relevant gene modifier of DYT1.

subject: Risch et al. (2007)
object: Risch et al. (2007) noted that the DYT1 GAG deletion is a major cause of early-onset dystonia, but only 30% of mutation carriers express clinical disease.

subject: Frédéric et al. (2008)
object: Frédéric et al. (2008) carried out a nationwide census of French TOR1A mutation carriers, studying 53 index cases and 104 relatives. They estimated the disease frequency of early-onset torsion dystonia due to TOR1A in France at 0.13 per 100,000 and the mutation frequency at 0.17 per 100,000, and concluded that the disease is rare in France.

subject: Frédéric et al. (2008)
object: In haplotype analysis of 53 French families carrying the recurrent TOR1A mutation, Frédéric et al. (2008) found the previously reported Ashkenazi Jewish haplotype in 11 families. The remaining families carried distinct haplotypes, which the authors suggested reflected independent mutation events.

subject: TOR1A unique and recurrent mutation in the TOR1A gene
object: TOR1A

subject: Zirn et al. (2008)
object: In a patient with early-onset DYT1 dystonia, Zirn et al. (2008) identified a c.863G>A transition in exon 5 of the TOR1A gene by sequencing, resulting in an arg288-to-gln (p.Arg288Gln) substitution in subdomain alpha-5 of TOR1A. The change was absent from 1,000 control chromosomes, and Arg288 is conserved throughout vertebrate evolution. The authors suggested that this may be a novel pathogenic TOR1A mutation in DYT1.

subject: Zirn et al. (2008)
object: Zirn et al. (2008) found that HEK293 cells overexpressing TOR1A with the p.Arg288Gln mutation showed an enlarged perinuclear space, the same morphologic change seen in cells overexpressing the common delta-GAG TOR1A mutation but not in cells overexpressing wildtype TOR1A.

subject: Kamm et al. (2008)
object: Kamm et al. (2008) reported that the D216H polymorphism modified susceptibility to DYT1 dystonia in European patients.

subject: Contarino et al. (2008)
object: Contarino et al. (2008) described a large 3-generation Dutch family from a small village on a former island with primary focal dystonia. Of the 24 family members examined, 8 were definitely affected and 4 were possibly affected. Mutations in the DYT1 gene and the SGCE gene were not detected, and linkage to the DYT6, DYT7, DYT13 and DYT16 loci was excluded, indicating genetic heterogeneity.

subject: Contarino et al. (2008)
object: In the Dutch focal dystonia family reported by Contarino et al. (2008), the affected members had mild cranio-cervical-brachial dystonia. Mean age at onset was 45.5 years (range, 39 to 56 years), the mean BFMDRS motor score was 4.4 (range, 1 to 8), and the mean TWSTRS part I score was 11.3 (range, 8 to 23).

subject: Carbon et al. (2009)
object: Carbon et al. (2009) used [11C]raclopride PET to study manifesting and nonmanifesting carriers of the DYT1 and DYT6 dystonia mutations and found significant reductions in caudate and putamen D2 receptor availability in both groups of mutation carriers relative to healthy controls. The reductions were greater in DYT6 than in DYT1 carriers (-38.0% vs -15.0%), and there was no significant difference between manifesting and nonmanifesting carriers of either genotype.

subject: Carbon et al. (2009)
object: Carbon et al. (2009) found by voxel-based analysis reduced raclopride binding in the ventrolateral thalamus of both DYT1 and DYT6 mutation carriers, more pronounced in DYT6 carriers and not influenced by clinical manifestation. The authors concluded that reduced D2 receptor availability is compatible with dysfunction or loss of D2-bearing neurons, increased synaptic dopamine, or both, and likely represents a susceptibility factor for developing clinical manifestations in mutation carriers.

subject: Calakos et al. (2010)
object: Calakos et al. (2010) reported a man in his fifth decade of life who had had involuntary jaw movements and grimacing for 3 years, consistent with oromandibular dystonia. He had bipolar disorder treated with lithium, remote exposure to dopamine receptor-blocking agents, cogwheel tone without rigidity, a mild action/postural tremor of the upper extremities, and absent Achilles reflexes. Brain MRI and laboratory studies were normal. His family history was negative for dystonia but included tremor and depression, and the movements responded well to anticholinergic agents.

subject: Calakos et al. (2010)
object: In a man with late-onset focal (oromandibular) dystonia, Calakos et al. (2010) sequenced TOR1A and found a heterozygous novel missense mutation in exon 3, c.613T>A (p.F205I). The variant was not present in 800 population controls (1,600 chromosomes). It affects a highly conserved phenylalanine in a beta strand of the AAA domain, and SIFT predicted it to be pathogenic (score 0.03). The authors suggested that the variant may contribute to the expression of dystonia.

subject: Calakos et al. (2010)
object: Calakos et al. (2010) expressed EGFP-tagged TOR1A in BHK cells. Inclusions formed in 44% of cells expressing the F205I mutant, 79% expressing deltaE, and 10% expressing wildtype. F205I inclusions were larger than deltaE inclusions and colocalized mostly with the ER marker KDEL (96%) rather than the nuclear envelope marker LaminB1 (19%), whereas deltaE inclusions colocalized with LaminB1 (89%). The authors concluded that F205I impairs TOR1A function but that its pathophysiology probably differs from that of deltaE.

subject: Calakos et al. (2010)
object: Calakos et al. (2010) suggested that the cellular differences between the F205I and deltaE TOR1A mutants may reflect the milder clinical phenotype (late-onset focal dystonia) of the patient carrying F205I, compared with the early-onset generalized dystonia caused by deltaGAG.
